item.title: Historic ballot sends Mirza Fakhrul to Bangabhaban
item.description:
Bangladesh elected its president through a parliamentary vote for the first time in nearly 35 years on Thursday, with BNP candidate Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir defeating opposition contender Col (retd) Oli Ahmad by a commanding 255-88 margin to become the country’s 23rd president.
The election ended more than three decades of uncontested presidential races and marked another major turn in Fakhrul’s political career after around 15 years at the helm of the BNP as its secretary general.
Chief Election Commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin, who served as returning officer, announced the result after voting ended at 5pm at the National Parliament.
“Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has secured 255 votes. I declare that, having received the highest number of votes, he has been duly elected president,” Nasir Uddin announced.
The Election Commission subsequently issued a gazette notification formally declaring Fakhrul president.
Of 349 eligible lawmakers, 343 cast their votes. Fakhrul received 255 votes, while Oli, the candidate of the Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party opposition alliance, secured 88.
Six lawmakers did not vote — BNP MPs Mirza Abbas, Mostafa Kamal Pasha and Dr Muhammad Osman Faruk; independent MP Rumeen Farhana; Jamaat MP Gazi Nazrul Islam; and Islami Andolan Bangladesh MP Md Oli Ullah.
The announcement triggered celebrations inside the Parliament Chamber, with lawmakers thumping their desks as Fakhrul raised his hand to acknowledge their congratulations.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman presented the president-elect with a red rose before shaking hands and embracing him.
In a notable display of political cordiality after the contest, Leader of the Opposition Dr Shafiqur Rahman and Deputy Leader of the Opposition Syed Abdullah Mohammed Taher approached the treasury bench with other opposition lawmakers.
Fakhrul left his seat and embraced Shafiqur.
Tarique then embraced Fakhrul, while the prime minister and opposition leader also exchanged an embrace.
Lawmakers from the treasury and opposition benches subsequently exchanged greetings as the chamber took on a celebratory atmosphere.
Fakhrul later shook hands with CEC Nasir Uddin and greeted election officials.
Bangabhaban is preparing to hold the oath-taking ceremony for the new president on Friday evening.
Voting took place from 2pm to 5pm through an open ballot.
Acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmad and acting Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal cast their votes at 2:10pm, followed a minute later by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Fakhrul.
With the Chittagong-4 seat vacant, 349 lawmakers were eligible to vote.
The National Parliament currently has 247 BNP MPs, 77 from Jamaat, eight from NCP, eight independents, three from Bangladesh Khilafat Majlis, and one each from Bangladesh Jatiya Party-BJP, Gono Odhikar Parishad, Ganosamhati Andolon, Khilafat Majlis, Islami Andolan Bangladesh and Jatiya Ganatantrik Party.
The BNP-led ruling camp commands 250 seats, while the 11-party opposition alliance has 90.
The result nevertheless showed Fakhrul receiving five votes more than the ruling camp’s stated strength, while Oli received two fewer than the opposition alliance’s 90 seats.
With six lawmakers absent, the open-ballot result provides an unusual glimpse of votes crossing the formal political divide.
The previous contested presidential election was held on October 8, 1991, when BNP candidate Abdur Rahman Biswas defeated Awami League candidate Badrul Haider Chowdhury by 172 votes to 92.
Every presidential election since then had ended without a ballot because only one candidate remained in contention.
Thursday’s election was triggered by Mohammed Shahabuddin’s resignation on July 24, after which Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad assumed responsibility as acting president.
Under Article 123(2) of the Constitution, an election must be held within 90 days when the presidency falls vacant following a resignation.

item.title: Congratulations pour in for Fakhrul
item.description:
Congratulations poured in from political leaders, foreign missions and prominent figures on Thursday evening after Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was elected Bangladesh’s 23rd president, with messages expressing hopes that the veteran politician would uphold democracy, justice and the dignity of the country’s highest constitutional office.
Nobel laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Opposition Leader Dr Shafiqur Rahman and Fakhrul’s presidential rival Col (retd) Oli Ahmad were among those congratulating him, while China and the United Kingdom were among the first foreign partners to publicly welcome his election.
Fakhrul defeated Oli, the candidate of the Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party opposition alliance, by 255 votes to 88 in Thursday’s presidential election, the first contested race for Bangabhaban in nearly 35 years.
The Election Commission subsequently issued a gazette declaring him elected president.
Professor Yunus extended his “heartfelt congratulations and best wishes” to Fakhrul, describing his political career of more than five decades as closely intertwined with Bangladesh’s political history.
He said: “His organizational skills, wisdom, leadership during times of crisis, and extensive experience working closely with people at the grassroots level have established him as a distinctive figure in the country’s national politics.”
Yunus expressed confidence that Fakhrul’s background as an academic, seasoned politician and “man of principle” would help him further uphold the dignity of the presidency.
He said: “I look forward to Bangladesh advancing towards greater prosperity, justice, and democracy under the leadership of President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir. I wish his excellency good health, a long life, and every success in the discharge of his responsibilities.”
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was among the first to congratulate Fakhrul immediately after the result was announced inside the National Parliament.
Tarique shook hands with Fakhrul, presented him with a red rose and later embraced him as lawmakers thumped their desks in congratulations.
The celebrations also produced a display of political cordiality across the aisle, with opposition leaders approaching the treasury bench after the result.
Opposition Leader and Jamaat Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman congratulated Fakhrul and expressed hope that he would use his “utmost ability and wisdom” to uphold justice and democracy and protect Bangladesh’s independence and sovereignty.
“I extend my heartfelt congratulations to Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on being elected the 23rd president,” Shafiqur said in a Facebook post.
Col (retd) Oli Ahmad also congratulated Fakhrul after losing the presidential contest.
In a message, the LDP chairman expressed hope that Fakhrul would uphold the Constitution and discharge his responsibilities with firmness and competence while safeguarding independence, democracy and justice.
Oli also wished him good health and a long life.
The gesture came after a rare competitive presidential election. Bangladesh had not witnessed a contested vote for the presidency since 1991.
Foreign congratulations also began arriving shortly after Fakhrul’s victory.
The Chinese Embassy in Dhaka said: “Warm congratulations to Mirza Fakharul Islam Alamgir on his election as president of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh.”
China said it attached great importance to its relationship with Bangladesh and was ready to work closely with Dhaka to deepen bilateral cooperation and deliver greater benefits to the peoples of both countries.
The British High Commission also congratulated Fakhrul, signalling its intention to work with the new head of state.
It said: “The UK looks forward to working with Hon. President Fakhrul and the Government of Bangladesh to further strengthen the close and longstanding partnership between our two countries.”
As of Thursday evening, searches of current published reports found these as the principal publicly reported congratulations; additional messages from foreign governments and political leaders may follow after Fakhrul formally takes office.
The 78-year-old veteran politician is expected to be sworn in on Friday evening, completing his transition from longtime BNP secretary general and Cabinet minister to Bangabhaban.

item.title: 22 years on, August 21 wounds remain, justice question returns
item.description:
Twenty-two years after grenades rained down on an Awami League rally at Bangabandhu Avenue, survivors of one of Bangladesh’s deadliest political attacks are marking another August 21 with the physical and psychological scars still intact, but with the legal case ending in the acquittal of all those convicted by the trial court.
The August 21, 2004 attack killed 24 people and injured more than 100 as grenades exploded at a rally addressed by then opposition leader Sheikh Hasina.
More than two decades later, survivors say their struggle has moved beyond the injuries they suffered that afternoon to questions of justice, financial hardship and, for some, a new life of insecurity.
For Md Anwar Parvez Tinku, an eyewitness and injured survivor, the memories remain vivid.
Recalling the moments before the attack, he said Sheikh Hasina had climbed onto a truck to address the rally, surrounded by senior Awami League leaders, when the explosions began.
He said: “Apa was going to give a speech on the microphone, at that moment grenades started exploding like rain. We scattered like flower petals everywhere. Leaders and activists formed a human shield to save Apa. Blood flowed all around, heads, hands and feet of many present were scattered around. It felt like my right leg had been blown off.”
Twenty-two years later, Tinku said the trauma still follows him into his sleep.
He said: “After the grenade attack, the police there did not take us to the hospital either. They fired tear gas. I was severely injured in the grenade attack on my right leg.”
Doctors at several hospitals recommended amputating his leg, he said, before another physician managed to save it through surgery. But the injuries continue to affect his life.
“I am suffering from leg pain, and besides, I have a bomb scar on my body. I cannot do any work. I am somehow surviving with a daughter and a wife. My brothers pay some expenses every month, so I go on. Due to lack of money, I cannot even get my leg treated,” he said.
The anniversary comes against a dramatically changed legal backdrop.
In October 2018, Dhaka’s Speedy Trial Tribunal-1 sentenced 19 people, including former state minister for home affairs Lutfuzzaman Babar and former deputy minister Abdus Salam Pintu, to death.
Another 19, including Tarique Rahman, were sentenced to life imprisonment, while 11 others received varying prison terms.
But the convictions were subsequently overturned.
The High Court acquitted all those convicted in the cases, and on September 4, 2025, a six-member Appellate Division bench unanimously dismissed the state’s appeal, leaving the acquittals intact.
The legal reversal has left survivors such as Tinku questioning whether they will ever see anyone held responsible.
He said: “Many of our comrades have been killed and injured. The murder of those who were killed has not been tried yet. I want to see the trial of those who ordered, financed and planned the grenade attack before they die. This will give peace to the souls of our fallen comrades.”
For some survivors, the political upheaval following the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024 has brought another layer of hardship.
Several victims, who wished to remain anonymous due to safety concerns, told Dhaka Tribune that they had subsequently been implicated in criminal cases, while some had gone into hiding.
They alleged their homes had been attacked or burned and their families were struggling financially.
Some said they were working anonymously as rickshaw pullers or labourers to survive.
One woman injured in the grenade attack described the desperation of living with both the old wounds and her present circumstances.
She said: “I have come back from the door of death. However, it was better to die. It is difficult to survive the lawsuit and police harassment. I have no money to eat, how can I file a case?”
Some survivors are also critical of the former Awami League government, saying it had years in power to ensure a definitive judicial conclusion to the attack.
They said the injured were repeatedly brought before television cameras around August 21, but their suffering became entangled with partisan politics rather than producing lasting closure.
The attack itself has passed into Bangladesh’s political history.
Its judicial journey has travelled from investigation and trial to mass convictions, appeals and ultimately the acquittal of all those convicted.
Yet for those who were standing on Bangabandhu Avenue 22 years ago, August 21 is not merely history.
The court cases may have reached their legal conclusion, but survivors still carry grenade splinters, disabilities and memories of the dead.
For them, another anniversary arrives with the most fundamental question still unsettled: who will ultimately be held accountable for August 21?

item.title: ‘Investors can’t underwrite a company in a market they can’t picture’
item.description:
Hussain Elius, co-founder of Pathao, speaks to Dhaka Tribune’s Wafiur Rahman about life after Pathao, the structural problems holding back Bangladesh’s startup ecosystem, lessons from building one of the country’s biggest tech companies, and the void left by his friend and early backer Fahim Saleh.
Since Pathao, I started Wind, a cross-border payments company built on blockchain rails. The pitch is simple: move money across borders faster, cheaper and more transparently than the correspondent banking system, which typically charges 3% to 5% and settles slowly. The company was acquired by Fin.com in the US in 2024.
The difference from Pathao wasn’t just the product; it was the entire operating mode. Pathao was a street fight: riders, red helmets, no rulebook, building trust with a population that had never split a fare with an app before.
Wind is quieter and more technical. There are no drivers to onboard or traffic police to negotiate with. Instead, there are compliance regimes, banking partners and licensing conversations, because this time we’re moving other people’s money, not just their packages.
I also recently released Moving Bangladesh: The Origin Story of Pathao, a business book and biography about how we built the company. It is the unfiltered, tactical reality of scaling Pathao, not the version that ends up in press releases, and the lessons we learned from building one of Bangladesh’s largest tech companies.
I’ll caveat this properly: I’ve been out of the operating seat since 2021, so take this as an informed outsider’s read, not an insider’s.
The opportunity is that the current funding winter is brutal for the ecosystem, but it’s arguably good news for the strongest incumbent in it.
When capital is scarce, weaker, capital-dependent competitors get forced into the open -- unpaid wages, shrinking headcounts, emergency requests to state funds.
Pathao has already survived its own near-death experience in 2019 and came out the other side disciplined about unit economics. It is structurally in a better position to consolidate market share while others are just trying to make payroll.
That’s a speculative read on my part, since I don’t have their internal numbers anymore, but it’s consistent with how these cycles usually play out.
The challenge is that the ceiling I wrote about in the book hasn’t moved. Bangladesh is roughly three cities’ worth of addressable ride and delivery demand.
Rapido in India expanded into a hundred cities and is now worth multiples of Pathao’s peak valuation, largely because India kept giving them a next city to enter.
Pathao’s fourth market was Nepal, not because it was the biggest opportunity, but because it was the only one left that made sense to reach without a bigger balance sheet.
Whatever Pathao does next -- fintech, deeper logistics infrastructure for the rest of the ecosystem, more of Nepal -- it has to solve the same problem I never fully solved: how do you build something Bangladesh-sized into something regionally or globally sized without the capital that usually funds that jump?
Yes, and it’s not the thing people usually guess. It wasn’t the spending, the hiring pace or even the layoffs. Those were mistakes too, but they were forced mistakes, made under real constraints.
The real one was this: when we had the cash and momentum to push into a genuinely large market, we expanded into a small one.
We went to Nepal instead of India.
At the time, it was the obviously sensible choice -- geographically close, culturally similar, and our playbook ported over almost unchanged.
That’s exactly what made it the wrong call.
By the time I understood what that decision cost us, cheap global capital had dried up. Grab and Gojek had Southeast Asia locked down, while Uber, Ola and Rapido had India locked down. We didn’t have the runway or the energy to fight a second war in someone else’s backyard.
If I’m being honest with myself, that single choice -- safe over ambitious, at the one moment we had the resources to be ambitious -- mattered more to Pathao’s ceiling than any operational decision we made in seven years.
The answer isn’t about talent or ideas. It’s about what happens after a startup runs out of money, or after it needs a real exit.
In deep-capital markets, a struggling company has options: a strategic buyer, a bridge round, sometimes even a public listing on growth metrics alone.
In Bangladesh, none of those exist at scale. The public market isn’t deep enough for a real tech IPO. There’s no meaningful base of strategic acquirers.
The local investor community is small and genuinely risk-averse, not irrationally so; they just don’t have the balance sheets to absorb frontier-market losses. And foreign capital shows up late, conditional on proof that a cash-burning company usually can’t produce yet.
I call this the “Bangladesh Tax”: every company here that depends on outside capital to survive pays it, one way or another.
There’s a second, less visible layer: the LP mandate problem.
Global venture capital doesn’t flow because a fund manager personally likes your pitch. It flows because a fund has a documented mandate -- geography, stage, sector -- that a pension fund or endowment board signed off on.
Bangladesh, for most of the last decade, simply wasn’t inside anyone’s mandate.
That’s not a judgment on the quality of the founders or ideas. It is a structural fact about how institutional capital gets allocated.
Every market that eventually gets a mandate -- Vietnam, Indonesia a decade ago -- started without one. Someone has to be the first deal that gives the next fund a comparable to point to when they go back to their own LPs.
I’d separate two things that are easy to conflate here: sentiment and mandate.
Sentiment has clearly gotten worse in the short term.
Chaldal was, by reputation, one of the most disciplined operators in the country, and its 2026 liquidity crisis -- unpaid wages, protests outside the Jessore facility, a Tk40 crore working-capital shortfall, an emergency request to Startup Bangladesh that reportedly fell through -- is being read by longtime sceptics as vindication that the whole “startup boom” narrative was overstated.
That reaction is happening in real time on social media and in the trade press, and it’s not helping anyone currently raising.
But the deeper issue, the mandate problem I mentioned earlier, was never really about perception, and I don’t think one company’s stress, however prominent, moves it much either way.
Bangladesh not being inside most global funds’ investable geography wasn’t a verdict on Chaldal, Pathao or ShopUp specifically. It was a structural fact before any of these companies existed.
My somewhat speculative read is that Chaldal’s troubles will sting locally and will be cited by critics for a while, but they’re unlikely to be the deciding factor in whether international capital allocators add Bangladesh to their mandates.
What actually moves that needle is a handful of clean, comparable exits, the kind that let a fund manager tell their own LPs: “This is a known, investable category now.”
We haven’t had enough of those yet.
A few things I wish someone had told me plainly when I started out.
First, understand the fundraising stack and don’t skip layers. Most advice jumps straight from “get an angel” to “raise a Series A” as if they sit next to each other. They don’t.
There’s a middle layer, expert individual capital without a fund’s formal structure: super angels, family offices, people who invest on conviction and relationships rather than a mandate. Know which layer you’re actually talking to, and pitch accordingly.
Second, a “no” is often about the fund’s mandate, not your company. Some of the sharpest investors I sat across from passed on Pathao, not because the analysis was weak, but because their fund’s structure genuinely couldn’t hold a frontier-market position on the timeline required.
Don’t over-update on a rejection without knowing which kind it was.
Third, sell the market before you sell the company if you’re outside the mapped geographies. I used to walk into rooms in Singapore and spend the first 20 minutes explaining why Bangladesh mattered before I ever got to Pathao.
That’s still true for most Bangladeshi founders today.
Investors can’t underwrite a company in a market they can’t picture.
Fourth, build the unit economics story before you build the growth story. The single best piece of advice I ignored came from a Russian investor who told me in 2018 to “be a cockroach, not a unicorn.”
Know your break-even volume for every product line before you launch the next one.
Investors trust a founder who’s choosing to grow faster with their capital far more than one who needs it to survive.
Finally, fundraise yourself. Don’t outsource it. Every time I’ve seen a founder hand fundraising to an external hire or a CFO, it’s gone badly.
No one can sell your company’s conviction the way you can, and no serious investor backs a company whose CEO isn’t personally the one asking.
Fahim was the first person who bet on me, before there was a “Bangladesh startup ecosystem” for anyone to bet on.
He said yes to sponsoring a joke website I made for $200 before he’d ever met me. That instinct, seeing a person rather than a market, isn’t something institutional capital is built to do.
Without him, I don’t know if I aim as high, as early, or if I ever end up in the rooms that eventually built Pathao.
What his death took from Bangladesh’s startup scene is harder to see from the outside, and I think it’s the part that gets missed.
Fahim wasn’t only backing Pathao. He was the person a handful of other founders called when a round wasn’t closing, when a key hire fell through, when someone needed a person who’d actually done it to tell them it was going to be okay.
When he died, that support beam went with him.
Some of those companies made it through anyway. Most didn’t.
The real cost isn’t just the companies he built; it’s the companies that never got the chance to start because the person who would have made the first, irrational, conviction-based bet on them wasn’t there anymore.
That’s a harder loss to put a number on than anything on a cap table.

item.title: New pay scale nears final stage, Cabinet to decide rollout
item.description:
A new salary structure covering around two million government employees, pensioners and other beneficiaries has moved closer to implementation, with the Cabinet now set to decide when it will take effect and whether the financial burden will be spread over multiple phases.
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir said on Thursday that two major stages of the pay-scale process had already been completed and work was progressing towards a final Cabinet decision.
“The work is underway. The Cabinet will decide everything soon,” Titumir told reporters at the Secretariat.
The development comes as the government weighs the substantial fiscal implications of higher salaries and pensions against inflationary pressure that has eroded the purchasing power of public servants.
Titumir said around 1.4 million government officials and employees currently receive basic salaries.
Once pensioners and other related beneficiaries are included, the new structure could affect around two million people.
Under the process, the Pay Service Commission and the relevant pay committee for the armed forces have submitted their reports, which have been reviewed by the secretary-level committee with recommendations.
A Cabinet-formed committee is separately examining the salary structure for the judiciary.
Its first meeting has already been held, and recommendations will be prepared considering Bangladesh’s fiscal realities, the sensitivity of the issue and constitutional obligations.
The proposals will then go before the Cabinet, which will determine the effective date and whether the new pay structure will be implemented at once or in phases.
Titumir said inflation was being considered while designing the new structure, particularly its impact on government employees and pensioners.
However, he cautioned against assuming that higher government salaries would automatically reduce corruption, saying the objective was to establish an effective and reasonable compensation system.
He also argued that public and private-sector salaries should not be compared mechanically, as responsibilities and employment structures differ.
Borrowing not ruled out
Asked whether the government could borrow to finance the new pay structure, Titumir said borrowing itself should not be viewed negatively; the critical questions were its cost, purpose and economic return.
He said: “Can any business run without loans? Loan is not an issue. The issue is what percentage of the budget deficit is and what percentage of the gross domestic product is being collected in taxes.”
“We need to see at what interest, from whom, and for how long it is being taken,” he added.
The government, he said, would also have to consider spending on health, education and social protection, alongside whether fiscal policies were encouraging private investment and employment.
Titumir stressed increasing domestic resource mobilisation rather than simply raising tax rates, while criticising what he described as misleading economic narratives and information in the past.
Fuel buffer stock planned
Turning to the energy crisis, Titumir said the government expected some relief during winter and more visible improvement by next summer, while targeting broader energy security by 2029.
The government is considering establishing a mandatory fuel buffer stock to protect the country against future supply disruptions, drawing lessons from the current crisis.
“If the necessary stocks were kept in the past, the scale of the crisis would not have been so great,” he said.
Similar to strategic stocks of rice and wheat maintained for food security, he said Bangladesh needed minimum reserve standards for electricity-generation fuels to cushion the economy against international crises and sudden supply disruptions.
The government is also exploring alternative LNG sources and transportation routes amid supply complications, including discussions with Qatar and other potential suppliers.
Titumir said new offshore oil and gas exploration blocks were being prepared, with the government planning to move towards a tender process by November.
The government is also seeking to reduce financial liabilities in future power-sector agreements through a “No Power, No Pay” principle, under which producers would not receive payments when electricity is not generated.
The immediate focus, however, remains the new pay structure.
With the technical stages advancing, the politically and fiscally consequential decisions -- when it begins, how quickly it is rolled out and how the government pays for it -- now rest with the Cabinet.

item.description:
Health officials on Wednesday said they recorded 671 fresh cases of dengue onslaughts killing at least two persons in the past 24 hours.
"During the period, (of the 671) 70 patients were hospitalized in Barisal division, 83 in Chittagong division, 119 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and 130 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, 133 in Khulna division, 35 in Mymensingh division, 92 in Rajshahi division and six in Rangpur division and three in Sylhet division, a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement said.

The dengue last year claimed 413 lives and inflicted 1,02,861 people in the country.

item.title: Private clinics mushroom across Naogaon, raising regulatory concerns
item.description:
Private hospitals, clinics and diagnostic centres have mushroomed across Naogaon’s 11 upazilas, raising concerns over facilities allegedly operating without proper documents and approvals.
Many of these establishments have reportedly been operating for years despite lacking the required paperwork, while authorities often appear to step up enforcement only after serious incidents, including patient deaths allegedly linked to medical negligence.
Once administrative drives subside, however, some of the facilities reportedly resume operations.
Several private establishments also lack the infrastructure and environment required to provide proper medical care, raising concerns about patient safety.
The proliferation of private facilities around government upazila health complexes has added to the problem. Patients and locals allege that brokers representing private hospitals, clinics and diagnostic centres remain stationed around government hospitals to divert patients to private facilities.
There are also allegations that some doctors working at government health complexes have arrangements with private hospitals, clinics and diagnostic centres.
Patients from remote areas seeking treatment at government facilities are sometimes allegedly pushed into undergoing unnecessary diagnostic tests, even when they seek treatment for common ailments.
Patients have also complained about the behaviour of some government doctors, shortages of medicines and the irregular availability of physicians. They said these problems have contributed to growing dissatisfaction with government healthcare services.
By contrast, private facilities are often perceived as offering more attentive care and better treatment to patients in exchange for payment, encouraging more people to seek treatment there.
According to the Naogaon Civil Surgeon’s Office, the district has 115 registered private hospitals and clinics across its 11 upazilas. Naogaon Sadar has the highest number, with 43.
An application has recently been submitted to establish a facility named Science Lab and Hospital in Naogaon Sadar.
Meanwhile, Ekta Clinic at Saraigachhi intersection in Porsha and Porsha Islami Lab and Hospital have been ordered to shut down, according to the Civil Surgeon’s Office.
Civil Surgeon Dr Md Aminul Islam said the health department was working to bring greater transparency to the district’s healthcare sector.
“Whenever we receive allegations or find irregularities involving private hospitals, clinics or diagnostic centres, we conduct drives and take immediate action,” he said.
He said the district’s healthcare services had improved significantly compared with the past.
The health department would continue its efforts to eliminate irregularities, the civil surgeon said, urging people with specific complaints to submit them in writing so authorities could investigate and take appropriate action.

item.title: 82% of children who died from measles lacked exclusive breastfeeding
item.description:
About 82% of children who died while undergoing treatment for measles had not received adequate or exclusive breastfeeding during their first 6 months of life, according to a joint study by Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute and icddr,b.
The findings were presented at a dissemination meeting on the study at the auditorium of Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka, on Wednesday.
The study was conducted among 354 children hospitalized with measles and is still ongoing, researchers said.
According to the study, 40% of the affected children were aged between 3 and 9 months. Overall, 38% had not received exclusive breastfeeding during the first 6 months of life.
The proportion was significantly higher among children who died while undergoing treatment, with 82% not having received exclusive breastfeeding during their first 6 months.
Researchers also analyzed the nutritional status of the children. The study found that 65% of measles-affected children were malnourished, including 12% with severe malnutrition and 53% with moderate malnutrition.
For an analysis based on age and vaccination status, researchers divided 341 children into 4 groups.
Among 146 children under 9 months of age who were not yet eligible for routine measles vaccination, 142 tested positive for measles, representing 97.3%.
Among 126 children who were eligible for vaccination but had not received any dose, 122 tested positive, or 97%.
Of the 48 children who had received 1 dose of vaccine, 44 tested positive for measles, representing 92%. Meanwhile, 16 of the 21 children who had received the recommended 2 doses tested positive, accounting for 76%.
Researchers cautioned that the finding does not mean that 76% of children who receive 2 doses of measles vaccine contract the disease.
The study was not conducted among the general population. Instead, it focused on a specific group of children admitted to hospital with suspected measles.
Therefore, the finding that 16 of the 21 suspected cases who had received 2 doses tested positive requires further investigation, researchers said.
The study noted that several factors may contribute to infection despite vaccination, including inadequate development of immunity after vaccination, waning antibody protection over time, malnutrition and other individual health-related factors.
However, determining the extent to which each factor contributed to infection was beyond the scope of the current study.
Researchers also analyzed the measles virus detected among the affected children. All the viruses identified belonged to the B3 subclade and showed similarities with B3 viruses detected in other countries.
The researchers also identified 4 changes or mutations in the epitope region of the virus's H protein, which can be recognized by antibodies.
The research was conducted under the Epidemiology and Research Department of Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute.
The main research paper was presented by the institute's Director Professor Dr Mirza Mohammad Ziaul Islam and icddr,b Senior Director Dr Mustafizur Rahman.
State Minister for Health and Family Welfare Dr MA Muhit attended the dissemination meeting as the chief guest, while Professor Dr AKM Azizul Haque, chairman of the governing board of Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, chaired the event.
Director General of the Directorate General of Health Services Professor Dr Prabhat Chandra Biswas, DGHS Director Dr Md Nurul Islam and IEDCR Director Dr Kazi Ahmed Zaki attended the meeting as special guests.

item.title: 30 injured as madrasa students clash with police in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
At least 30 people, including 24 madrasa students and six policemen, were injured in a clash between students of Darul Arkam Madrasa and police during a cultural program at the Brahmanbaria Police Lines on Tuesday night.
The incident occurred around 11:30pm inside the Police Lines in the western Medda area of the city after madrasa students reportedly complained about loud music being played at the program.
According to police, madrasa students and locals, the district police were organising the cultural program at the drill shed to mark the arrival of Chittagong Range DIG Abdul Quddus Chowdhury.
Students of the nearby Darul Arkam Madrasa reportedly complained that the loud music was disrupting their studies ahead of examinations scheduled for Wednesday.
Some students went to the Police Lines and asked police personnel to lower the volume. An argument subsequently broke out between the students and police.
As news of the altercation spread, more than 100 madrasa students entered the Police Lines, leading to heightened tensions.
Police then charged with batons to disperse the students, who responded by throwing stones, according to witnesses. The situation subsequently turned violent, with clashes reported inside and outside the Police Lines.
Some students of Darul Arkam Madrasa said they had been preparing for examinations when the loud music began disrupting their studies.
They said they initially approached police and requested that the volume be lowered. Although the music was turned down temporarily, they alleged that the volume was later increased again.
The students alleged that police subsequently charged them with batons when an argument broke out.
The injured students were taken to Brahmanbaria District Sadar Hospital and other hospitals for treatment.
District BNP General Secretary and Upazila Parishad Administrator Sirajul Islam Siraj visited the hospital with party leaders and activists and inquired about the injured students.
Later, madrasa students held a protest procession on several roads in the city and gathered in front of the Press Club for a protest rally. They demanded exemplary punishment for those responsible for the incident.
Around 3am, the Brahmanbaria Qawmi Chhatra Oikya Parishad placed a five-point demand in the presence of Police Superintendent Shah Md Abdur Rouf and District Council Administrator Sirajul Islam Siraj.
The demands include banning loud concerts at the Police Lines that disturb nearby institutions, reviewing CCTV footage and taking action against those responsible, ensuring proper treatment for the injured, implementing the demands by 10am and having the police superintendent take responsibility and issue an unconditional apology.
Brahmanbaria Police Superintendent Shah Md Abdur Rouf, who was present at the program, later visited the madrasa and said the incident resulted from a misunderstanding over the sound from the cultural program.
In a video message, he said the CCTV footage would be reviewed transparently and action would be taken against those found responsible or those who acted excessively.
“Many children have been injured because of a small misunderstanding. This is really unfortunate, and I feel bad about it,” he said.
The police superintendent said arrangements had been made for the injured to receive proper treatment and that necessary financial assistance would also be provided.
He said an investigation committee would be formed, with student representatives included, to examine the incident and ensure justice.
Maulana Sajidur Rahman, principal of Darul Arkam Madrasa and secretary general of Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh, also urged students and others to remain calm.
In a video message, he said the police superintendent and District Council Administrator Sirajul Islam Siraj had visited the madrasa and discussed the students’ demands.
He said the police superintendent had assured them that exemplary action would be taken against those responsible after reviewing the video footage.
Sajidur Rahman urged students, ulema and others concerned to remain calm, saying the matter would be properly investigated and justice ensured based on the footage.

item.title: BIP: Unplanned urbanisation pushes Dhaka near bottom of livability index
item.description:
Dhaka now ranks 171st among 173 cities on the Global Livability Index, planners said Tuesday warning that unplanned urbanisation, environmental degradation and weak governance have pushed the capital to one of the lowest livability levels in the world.
Speaking at a press conference titled "Dhaka City's Livability: Challenges and Roadmap for Planned Solutions," organised by the Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP) at its conference hall in Planners Tower, BIP President Muhammad Ariful Islam said transport, air and noise pollution, waterlogging, shrinking green space, public health risks and weak social inclusion are all directly tied to the city's planning failures.
He said Dhaka ranks 18th among the world's most polluted cities.
Of the roughly 56 canals the city once had, only 26 survive in any recognisable form, while 48 areas have been identified as waterlogging-prone due to encroachment on canals and wetlands and poor drainage, he said.
Ariful Islam said unplanned billboards and lighting are damaging the cityscape and road safety, he added, while rising building density and poor waste management are fuelling dengue and chikungunya risks.
Only 7.99 percent of the city's 99.29 square kilometres is green space, he said, far short of what a livable city needs.
On transport, Ariful said Dhaka loses about 50 lakh working hours annually to congestion, at an estimated economic cost of Tk 37,000 crore.
He said around 1,765 tonnes of waste, 27 percent of total generation, goes uncollected daily, worsening waterlogging and mosquito breeding.
BIP General Secretary Mohammad Mosleh Uddin Hasan said Dhaka is heading toward its lowest-ever livability level due to poor implementation of existing plans and institutional weakness.
Planner Adil Muhammad Khan raised concerns over footpath encroachment, illegal businesses, extortion, and political influence in urban management while planner AKM Riaz Uddin noted that despite declining livability, migration to Dhaka continues because other regions lack jobs and services.
Speakers agreed that Dhaka's crisis stems from interlinked failures in environment, land use, transport, health and waste management, calling for long-term, coordinated national planning.

item.title: HSBC launches Export Excellence Awards 2026
item.description:
The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (HSBC) in Bangladesh has officially launched the 10th edition of its flagship 'HSBC Export Excellence Awards 2026' to recognize and honor Bangladeshi exporters for their contributions to the nation’s sustainable economic growth.
The announcement was made during a press conference held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka.
The awards program will recognize high-performing businesses across four distinct categories based on annual export revenue thresholds:
Organized in partnership with the Ministry of Commerce and the British High Commission Dhaka, the awards will utilize Ernst & Young (EY) as an independent technical auditing partner.
Final selections will be evaluated by a joint jury board comprising representatives from HSBC’s senior leadership, the Ministry of Commerce, and the British High Commission.
Candidates will be assessed on financial performance, national economic contribution, operational diversity, corporate governance, regulatory compliance, and sustainable business practices.
Speaking at the launch, Md Mahbub ur Rahman, chief executive officer of HSBC Bangladesh, emphasized that the initiative honors trailblazing enterprises redefining the global footprint of "Made in Bangladesh" through innovation, quality, and long-term sustainability.

The awards program carries no entry fee or financial purse and is open to all operating enterprises across Bangladesh, regardless of whether they maintain an existing banking relationship with HSBC.
Eligible businesses and third-party nominators can submit entries online through the official portal ( www.business.hsbc.com .bd/EEA2026) until the nomination deadline on September 20, 2026.

item.title: AIUB hosts first-ever ‘QS Bangladesh Forum 2026’
item.description:
The first-ever QS Bangladesh Forum 2026 was held on Monday, August 17, at the Sheraton Dhaka, with the aim of advancing the future of higher education in Bangladesh, strengthening global standards, and enhancing the position of Bangladeshi universities in the international arena.
The forum was hosted by the American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB) and organized by QS (Quacquarelli Symonds), with support from the University Grants Commission of Bangladesh (UGC) and the Association of Private Universities of Bangladesh (APUB).
Themed “Benchmark Bangladesh: Building World-Class Universities Through Global Standards,” the forum brought together key stakeholders from Bangladesh’s higher education sector.
The inaugural session was attended by Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, MP, as chief guest.
Prof Mamun Ahmed, chairman of the University Grants Commission of Bangladesh, attended as guest of honour.
In his address, the minister highlighted the need to introduce PhD programs at private universities and indicated that initiatives would soon be taken in this regard.
Questioning why private universities should not be permitted to offer PhD programs, he emphasized the importance of creating broader opportunities for advanced research in the private higher education sector.
Referring to the development of private universities in Bangladesh since 1992, he stressed that, by 2026, the country must create greater opportunities for advanced research at private universities.
Highlighting the importance of research, he said that Bangladesh needs cross-border education and stronger research capacity in private universities.
He also noted that the country has no shortage of teachers and researchers, with thousands of researchers contributing to national development through knowledge, expertise, and “Made in Bangladesh” capabilities.
Prof Mamun Ahmed, chairman of UGC, said that Bangladeshi private universities still have significant room for improvement in global university rankings.
He emphasized the need for universities to take a leading role in improving academic quality and making their institutions more attractive to students. Such efforts, he noted, could help attract more international students to Bangladesh for higher education.
QS representatives also addressed the forum, including Ashwin Fernandes, vice president – strategic and international engagement, QS; Jason Newman, chief commercial officer, QS; and Rami Awad, director of regional partnerships, QS.
The welcome address was delivered by Ishtiaque Abedin, founding member of the board of trustees of AIUB and secretary general of APUB.
Md Sabur Khan, president of APUB, also addressed the forum.
The vote of thanks was delivered by Nadia Anwar, founding member and chairperson of the board of trustees, AIUB.
Following the inaugural session, three dedicated sessions were held on QS Rankings Methodology, QS ranking landscape of Bangladesh, and the QS Rankings 2028 Cycle.
The forum also featured two high-level panel discussions involving Vice-Chancellors from leading universities across Bangladesh: “From Campus to Capability: Closing Bangladesh’s Future Skills Gap in the AI Era” and “Accelerating Digital Transformation in Higher Education.”
The panel discussions focused on the future skills required by students in the age of artificial intelligence, aligning education with industry needs, leveraging technology in higher education, and accelerating digital transformation across universities.
The closing session featured a vote of thanks by Carmen Zita Lamagna, former vice chancellor, academic adviser, and member of the board of trustees, AIUB.
The QS Bangladesh Forum 2026 placed particular emphasis on the internationalization of higher education, enhancing the global visibility of research, improving student outcomes and capabilities, and strengthening international partnerships.
With the QS World University Rankings 2028 cycle ahead, discussions also focused on developing a common, practical, and strategic roadmap for universities to prepare for and improve their global competitiveness.

item.title: Jamuna Bank joins BB’s Tk10,000cr agriculture refinance scheme
item.description:
Jamuna Bank PLC has joined Bangladesh Bank’s Tk10,000 crore refinance scheme aimed at boosting agricultural production, strengthening food security and supporting the rural economy.
A participation agreement was signed between Bangladesh Bank and Jamuna Bank PLC on August 16.
Under the three-year revolving refinance scheme, financing will be available for a wide range of agriculture and rural activities, including crop production, fisheries, livestock, agricultural and irrigation machinery, and other income-generating activities.
Eligible farmers and customers will be able to access financing at a maximum simple interest rate of 8% per annum.
The agreement was signed by AKM Saiduzzaman, director, Agricultural Credit Department-2, Bangladesh Bank.
On Jamuna Bank’s behalf, deputy managing director & CRO Md Shahidul Islam and Md Abu Bakkar Siddique, head of agricultural loan, were present at the program.
Md Sakhawat Hossain, joint director-2, and Rafia Sultana, additional director of Bangladesh Bank’s Agricultural Credit Department, were also present at the ceremony.
Through its participation in the scheme, Jamuna Bank aims to expand access to affordable financing for farmers and rural entrepreneurs, helping increase agricultural production, generate employment and contribute to sustainable rural development.

item.title: Hop Lun partners with Brac Healthcare to host employee wellness camp
item.description:
Hop Lun Apparel Limited recently organized a comprehensive ‘Seasonal Disease Prevention and Awareness Session’ at its factory premises in partnership with Brac Healthcare.
The initiative provided workers with free medical check-ups as well as expert guidance on disease prevention, hygiene, and healthy living in order to safeguard their overall health and well-being.
During the session, workers underwent screenings for blood sugar, blood pressure and oxygen saturation levels.
Any individuals diagnosed with adverse health conditions were immediately provided medical treatment by Hop Lun’s in-house medical team.
Additionally, two healthcare professionals from Brac healthcare conducted interactive sessions with the workers, advising workers on preventing common illnesses, knowing when to consult a doctor, and effective ways to maintain overall health at home and in the workplace.
They discussed about how health and work are deeply connected and how personal physical fitness is key to both professional performance and personal life.
Dr Tahmid Hasan Probad, manager, QA and patient experience at Brac Healthcare Ltd, stated: “Through this partnership, we wanted to deliver quality healthcare access for workers and create health awareness among them. We firmly believe that a healthy worker thrives in the workplace with greater ease.”
Gulshan Ara, social initiatives head, Hop Lun Bangladesh, added: “The physical and mental well-being of our workers is one of our top priorities. With this initiative, we aimed to make essential medical support more accessible for our workers and to equip them with the knowledge they need in order to maintain proper health.”
Hop Lun Apparel Limited remains dedicated to prioritizing worker well-being and continuing such health and welfare initiatives across its facilities in the future.

item.title: Bangladesh, IOM launch new initiative to combat cyber-enabled human trafficking
item.description:
The International Organization for Migration (IOM-UN Migration) and the Economic Relations Division (ERD) of Ministry of Finance of Bangladesh have signed a 24-month project to strengthen Bangladesh's efforts to prevent and respond to human trafficking facilitated through digital technologies.
The project, "Countering Cyber-Enabled Human Trafficking Through Technology", funded by the IOM Development Fund, will be implemented by IOM Bangladesh in partnership with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The project aims to support longer-term efforts to prevent cyber-enabled human trafficking in Bangladesh. Its findings and training resources are expected to contribute to future policy and program development and to strengthen existing national and inter-agency efforts to combat trafficking, said a press release on Monday.
Responding to growing concerns over the use of social media, online platforms, job portals and other digital technologies by traffickers to target, recruit, control and exploit people, the project will focus on three key areas including building evidence and knowledge, strengthening law enforcement capacity and improving digital literacy in communities. The agreement was signed by Md Shahriar Kader Siddiky, secretary of ERD, and Dr Laura Tomm Bonde, chief of mission of IOM Bangladesh, in the presence of AKM Sohel, additional secretary and wing chief of UN Wing, ERD, and representatives of relevant government agencies including Ministry of Home Affairs and IOM, according to an ERD press release.
"Technology is transforming the way people communicate, seek employment and connect with opportunities, but it can also be exploited by traffickers," said Dr Laura Tomm Bonde. "This project will help strengthen the evidence, skills and community awareness needed to ensure that technology becomes part of the solution rather than a tool for exploitation," she added.
"The project will contribute to the Government of Bangladesh's efforts to prevent the misuse of technology for human trafficking while promoting technology as a means to counter human trafficking. Its overall outcome is to enable government stakeholders and communities to take informed action to prevent, respond to and mitigate the risks of cyber-enabled human trafficking," Md Shahriar Kader Siddiky emphasized.

item.title: Chamber court upholds bail for ex-chief justice Khairul Haque
item.description:
The Appellate Division’s Chamber Judge Court has upheld the High Court’s bail order for former chief justice A B M Khairul Haque in a case filed under the attempted murder and Explosives Act over violence during the July 2024 mass uprising.
Chamber Judge of the Appellate Division Justice Md Rezaul Haque passed a “no order” on Monday on a state petition seeking a stay on the High Court’s bail order.
Following the order, Khairul Haque’s lawyers said there is no longer any legal impediment to his release from jail.
Senior lawyer Motahar Hossain Saju appeared for Khairul Haque, assisted by lawyers Monayem Nabi Shaheen and others.
Earlier, on August 10, a High Court bench comprising Justice K M Zahid Sarwar and Justice Sheikh Abu Taher granted Khairul Haque bail in the case filed at Banani Police Station over the July uprising.
Khairul Haque was arrested from his Dhanmondi residence on July 24, 2025. He was later shown arrested in a case over the killing of Jubo Dal activist Abdul Qayyum Ahad in Jatrabari during the uprising and subsequently in several other cases.

item.title: 3 sentenced to death for killing AIUB student in Narayanganj
item.description:
A Narayanganj court on Monday sentenced three muggers to death for killing Wazed Alam Shimanto, a student of American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB), in 2024.
Narayanganj District and Sessions’ Judge Abu Shamim Azad pronounced the verdict.
The condemned convicts are Anik, Akash Khan and Chandi Babu.
According to the prosecution, three muggers intercepted Shimanto, a 2nd year student of the AIUB Department of Computer Science, in front of Morgan Girls’ High School at Deubhog of Narayanganj city around 6:00am on December 12, 2024.
At one stage, the hoodlums stabbed Shimanto indiscriminately and left the place after snatching his bag and mobile phone set.
The victim was sent to Dhaka Medical College Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries two days later.
Shimanto’s father Hazi Alam filed a case at Sadar Police Station in this regard.
Police arrested the trio from different parts of the district following the incident. All of them gave confessional statements before the court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

item.title: PM’s Adviser: 'Mob culture' will not be tolerated
item.description:
The government will not tolerate “mob culture” in the country and will enforce law to prevent such incidents, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Public Administration Affairs Ismail Zabihullah said on Monday.
“Mob culture is undesirable whenever it occurs. We hope there will be no mob culture, and it should never happen,” he said while responding to questions from journalists at an exchange of views at the Prime Minister’s Office in Tejgaon to mark 180 days of the government.
Asked about allegations that mob incidents continued after the ouster of Sheikh Hasina and that law enforcement agencies remained largely inactive in dealing with such incidents, the adviser said he had no clear example of a recent incident of the kind seen during the final period the interim government.
“There is no such mob culture as was seen toward the end of the interim government. However, we can assure you that this kind of mob culture will not be tolerated,” said Zabihullah, also a BNP Standing Committee member.
He stressed that the country would be governed according to law and that the government would enforce it.
Prime Minister’s Political Adviser and another BNP Standing Committee member Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, who joined the discussion, said the extent of mob culture has declined significantly.
He said such a culture emerged partly because of political support and that there had often been an indirect political influence behind such incidents.
“As the rule of law becomes stronger, mob violence will decline,” Rizvi said, adding that the government’s commitment to the rule of law would help create an environment in which such incidents would decrease further.
Prime Minister’s Office spokesperson Mahadi Amin presented statistics on the government’s activities and achievements over the past 180 days.
The event was moderated by Prime Minister’s Press Secretary Saleh Shibli. PM’s Political Adviser Nazrul Islam Khan, Political Adviser Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapan and Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon also spoke at the program.
Ministers and advisers responded to questions from journalists on various issues.
State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam, State Ministe for Information and Broadcasting Yaser Khan Chowdhury, Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir, Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant on Health SM Ziauddin Haider, Special Assistant on Environment, Forest and Climate Affairs Saimum Parvez and Chief Coordinator at the Prime Minister’s Office Prof SM Abdul Awal, among others, attended the program.

item.title: Hotel Sarina Dhaka brings flavours of Pakistan with Peshawari Food Festival
item.description:

The festival was inaugurated by Imran Haider, High Commissioner of Pakistan to Bangladesh, together with Zain Aziz, trade and investment attaché, and other officials of the Pakistan High Commission.
Representatives from leading media organizations, food bloggers and influencers were also invited to attend the inauguration.
Adding authenticity to the festival, Guest Chef Rai Abbas has specially travelled from Pakistan to curate and prepare a wide range of traditional specialties.
The buffet features favourites from different regions of Pakistan, including Nalli Pulao, Kabuli Pulao, Chicken Sanawari, Mutton Shajahani Handi, Beef Namkeen, Fish Hyderabadi Masala, Chicken Sindhi Biryani, Chicken Lahori Biryani, Chicken Yakhni Pulao and Peshawari Naan, along with many more traditional dishes.
A major attraction is the live cooking station, where famous Pakistani kebabs are freshly prepared and grilled for guests.
Alongside the Pakistani specialties, Summerfields’ continental and international buffet selections will also be available, offering an extensive dining experience for every palate.
The culinary experience has been curated to showcase the iconic flavours of Pakistan, with particular attention to traditional cooking techniques, aromatic spices and authentic regional recipes.
The festival aims not only to offer an exceptional dining experience but also to celebrate the cultural connection between Bangladesh and Pakistan through food and hospitality.

MoU signed to establish Gregorian Museum
item.description:
The Gregorian Society (TGS) has taken an initiative to preserve the rich history and heritage of St Gregory High School & College through the establishment of the Gregorian Museum under the slogan “Preserve and Conserve.”
An MoU for establishing the museum was recently signed between TGS and St Gregory High School & College. TGS Vice President and 1974-batch Gregorian Rizwan Khair and the school’s Principal Brother Placid Peter Rebeiro, CSC, signed the agreement on behalf of the two organisations.
The museum, which will be established on the school premises, is the result of years of dedicated efforts by former Gregorians from Bangladesh and around the world.
The initiative is expected to play an important role in preserving the history and heritage of the century-old institution, while showcasing its legacy and the achievements of its students to future generations.
The Gregorian Museum is scheduled to be formally inaugurated on November 13, 2026.

The 30-year-old midfielder will move for a fee of around 75 million euros ($87 million) according to reports.

Rodri had been linked with Real Madrid after Spain won the World Cup in July but Barcelona pushed to sign the former Atletico Madrid star, who has played a key part in Manchester City's success since he joined in 2019.
The midfielder, who won the Ballon d'Or in 2024, has struggled with injuries over the past two seasons but shone as Spain won their second World Cup.

item.title: Alex Emon murder: 3 arrested with firearms
item.description:
RAB-2 has arrested three people, including Md Hossain Ahmed Shahrukh, the second accused in the widely discussed Alex Emon murder case in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur.
They were arrested during separate operations in the Shahbagh and Rayerbazar areas on Saturday.
RAB-2 Commander Naimul Hasan disclosed the matter at a press briefing at the unit’s Mohammadpur headquarters.
The arrestees are: Md Hossain Ahmed Shahrukh, Md Tarekuzzaman Tarek, 30, and Md Shahidul Islam, 29.
RAB said an intelligence operation found that Shahrukh, a named accused in the case, and his associates were staying in Shahbagh. A team of RAB-2 later conducted a raid there and arrested the three.
Based on information obtained during interrogation, RAB later raided a house on Haji Yunus Khan Road in Rayerbazar.
The raid yielded a foreign-made 7.65mm pistol, a magazine, a locally made revolver, two rounds of ammunition, 260 grammes of gunpowder and two samurai swords, RAB said.
Naimul Hasan said several cases had previously been filed against Shahrukh with Mohammadpur Police Station, including two for theft, attempted robbery, attempted murder and intimidation; one for murder; one under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act; and one under the Speedy Trial Act.
Tarekuzzaman Tarek also has a case filed with Mohammadpur Police Station on charges of theft, attempted murder and intimidation, RAB said.
According to RAB, 11 people have so far been arrested in the Alex Emon murder case, including six named in the FIR and five others whose identities were initially unknown. Operations are ongoing to arrest the remaining suspects.

item.title: Info minister: Govt to establish Modern Information Complex in every district, upazila
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon has said the government is constructing modern information complex in every division.
The program will also be expanded at district and upazila level, he said while inaugurating the construction work of the modern Barisal Divisional Information Complex at Ichhakathi in Kashipur of Barisal city on Sunday.
The event was organized by the Department of Mass Communication under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
The information complexes will multifaceted centers for information, knowledge, entertainment and research, he said.
“The complexes will not only be eye-catching buildings; they will serve as hubs of information, knowledge and research. The complexes will primarily function as Digital Information Service Centers, providing a wide range of digital services to the public,” he said.
Swapon said development work under the project is already underway in 26 districts. To popularize the facilities and encourage students to engage in research, promotional leaflets will be distributed to local educational institutions through the ministry, he said.
“The government’s objective is not limited to infrastructure development; rather, it aims to bring the quality of the complexes up to international standard,” he said.
To achieve this, Swapon said, both infrastructure engineering and software engineering are being given separate and equal importance.
Highlighting the technological facilities planned for the complexes, Swapon said they would feature state-of-the-art, technology-enabled cineplexes and electronic screens, with facilities for screening digital movies as well as 3D and 4D films.
Speaking as chair of the event, Secretary of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting Mahbuba Farjana said the information complexes would play important role in combating misinformation and disinformation.
Barisal Divisional Commissioner Khalil Ahmed, Barisal City Corporation Administrator Advocate Bilkis Akter Jahan Shirin, spoke among others on the occasion.
In his welcome address, Project Director Moniruzzaman said the seven-storey modern Information Complex in Barisal is being constructed at a cost of Taka 17.63 crore.
Later, Deputy Project Director Rezaur Rabbi Moni presented details of the project through a multimedia presentation.

item.title: Model Ridhika Ridhi’s boyfriend sent to jail in suicide abetment case
item.description:
Model Ridhika Ridhi’s boyfriend, Hasibur Rahman, has been sent to jail in a case filed over her death at her Bashundhara Residential Area home in Dhaka. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Mahbub Alam passed the order on Sunday, said Prosecution Department Sub-Inspector Kamal Hossain.
Family members found Ridhi hanging from a ceiling fan in her bedroom on Saturday morning. She was rushed to Kurmitola General Hospital where doctors declared her dead.
Ridhi’s mother Moni Begum filed a case on the same day, accusing Hasibur of abetting her daughter’s suicide.
Hasibur, who had visited Ridhi’s home that day, was arrested from the spot.
On Sunday, Vatara police Sub-Inspector Abdul Wadud, the investigating officer, produced Hasibur before the court and sought his detention in jail.
In the petition, police said preliminary interrogation and investigation had yielded sufficient evidence supporting the allegations against Hasibur. They said he had confessed to the offence and admitted his involvement during questioning.
Police also expressed concern that he might flee if released on bail.
Hasibur’s lawyer, Golam Kibria Choton, sought bail and requested a hearing on Tuesday. The court sent Hasibur to jail and fixed Tuesday for the bail hearing. Police said Ridhi had been on a video call with Hasibur when the incident occurred. Although the death initially appeared to be a suicide, investigators are probing the circumstances to determine the exact cause of death.
Ridhi, who worked as a model, also acted in several dramas, including Ekhane Manush Bikri Hoy, Bahurupi, Double Honeymoon and Sundori.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 908 as 6 more die in 24hrs
item.description:
Six children died with measles-like symptoms in 24 hours until 8am on Sunday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 908 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all six latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With this, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 809, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 99.
A total of 1021 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 142,797.
Meanwhile, 80 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 17,880.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 124,457 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 119,939 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

item.title: Family Card brings relief to some, leaves Korail slum’s poorest behind
item.description:
Ahead of the 13th parliamentary election, the BNP pledged in its election manifesto to introduce the Family Card programme to strengthen the economic security of people, particularly women.
The government launched the pilot programme on March 10 at the T&T playground in Banani, adjacent to Dhaka’s Korail slum. Under the pilot programme, selected women receive Tk 2,500 a month through mobile financial services or bank accounts.
Since then, “Family Card” has become a familiar term among Korail residents. While the programme has brought relief to some families, many of the slum’s poorest residents say they have been left out.
Residents interviewed by Dhaka Tribune alleged that some relatively well-off households received the cards, while families struggling to afford even basic food were denied the benefit.
Rasheda, Morzina among those left out
Rasheda Begum, originally from Rangpur, has lived in Korail for more than a decade. With no homestead in her village, the slum has become her last refuge. She has two children, Tabassum and Zakaria. Tabassum has a disability. Rasheda begs on the streets and in the alleys around Mohakhali to support her children. Her husband left her after their child was born with a disability.
Despite applying for a Family Card, she did not receive one.
A similar story was shared by Morzina Khatun and her son Majnu, both of whom have physical disabilities. They have no homestead in their village and have lived in Korail for around 20 years.
Unable to walk, Morzina begs while sitting on a two-wheeled cart.
Rasheda and Morzina told Dhaka Tribune that officials collected their national ID details and photographs before the pilot programme began, but they received neither cards nor payments.
They alleged that many families with relatively better incomes received cards, while those struggling to afford three meals a day were left out.
“I eat when I can beg. Otherwise, I have to go without food,” Morzina said.
Rasheda said she had contemplated suicide because of poverty but was staying alive for her helpless children. Better-off families among beneficiaries
There is a contrasting picture in Korail, with some residents who appear relatively financially secure also receiving Family Cards.
Nasima Begum is one of them. Her husband, Ashraful, works as a school van driver. Nasima has a two-storey tin-roofed house in the slum with seven rooms, which she rents out for around Tk 5,000 each, earning about Tk 35,000 a month.
“I have received four months’ payments through the Family Card. But I have not received the payments for July and August yet,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
Poorest residents demand inclusion
During a visit to Beltola Adarsh Nagar in Korail on Saturday afternoon, this correspondent found tin-roofed shacks lining narrow lanes. Most homes are so cramped that there is barely enough space to stand inside.
Women in most households work as domestic workers or in garment factories. Many families have several children. In some households, husbands do not support their families, while in others, even the combined income of both spouses is insufficient to make ends meet.
For such families, the Family Card is a much-anticipated source of support.
Under the social safety-net programme, selected families receive cash through mobile financial services. But many households living alongside beneficiaries remain excluded.
Several residents who did not receive cards told Dhaka Tribune that elderly people, widows, persons with disabilities, people suffering from chronic illnesses and families without an earning member should receive priority.
They said only a few such families had received cards, while most remained excluded.
Disabled child, jailed husband leave Sharifa struggling
Sharifa Begum lives in Beltola Adarsh Nagar and works as a domestic helper. Her son Suman has a physical disability. His grandmother looks after him while Sharifa is at work. His father is currently in jail in connection with a case.
“I have done everything short of begging at people’s feet for a Family Card, but no one helped me. My husband is in jail. Even after working in people’s homes, I cannot afford two meals a day. I cannot afford treatment for my disabled child,” Sharifa said, wiping away tears.She appealed to the government for assistance for her son.
Alecha Begum, another extremely poor resident, also did not receive a card. Her husband is ill and unable to work. She earns a living doing domestic work. “I applied for a card but did not get one. Those who are better off got cards, but we did not,” she said.
Another resident, Jharna, said, “My husband’s income is not enough to run the family. I am struggling with two children. We desperately need a card.”
Four months’ payments received, July-August dues remain
Some beneficiaries received Tk 2,500 a month from March through June under the pilot programme, but several said they have yet to receive payments for July and August.
Marium Begum told Dhaka Tribune that she had received four months’ payments through mobile banking but had not received the payments for July and August.
Sharmin Begum said, “I have not received the money for two months, July and August. I went to the office to find out what happened, but they could not give me any information.”
PM to formally launch programme in Kishoreganj
Following the pilot phase, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to formally launch the Family Card programme in Kishoreganj on August 16. The launch is scheduled to take place at Ward 8 of Latifabad Union in Kishoreganj Sadar upazila.
Mohammad Rezaur Rahman, deputy director of the Department of Social Services, told Dhaka Tribune that the prime minister would formally launch the programme in Kishoreganj on August 16.
The programme will then be rolled out gradually across all upazilas and unions by the end of October.
Who will receive Family Cards?
Women from extremely poor, poor and low-income households will primarily be eligible for the cards, with extremely poor and poor families receiving priority during the initial phase.
Under the government guidelines, landless and homeless families, households with persons with disabilities, hijra and Bede communities, ethnic minority families and households owning up to 0.5 acres of land will receive priority.
A maximum of five members of each family will be considered for eligibility. In joint families, a separate card will be issued for every five members.
